However, if we bring in a hostile adversary that calculus changes, and you'd be right to start thinking about other approaches.

* https://hackmyclaw.com/ ; https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jun/26/hack-my-ai-assistant/

I'm not claiming auto is worse than manual; I'm claiming it cannot be compared with anything security-wise because it does not aim to provide any guarantees, there's no systematic way to reason about what it will and won't allow, etc

With e.g. VM or container sandboxing, we can say things like "If there are no vulnerabilities in the hypervisor or hardware, then the agent can only access these files, these network services, etc". Auto mode doesn't even try to provide any guarantees, so it's impossible to reason about. It amounts to just using the models judgment about what's "malicious" or not, a definition which is subjective, changes model to model, and can be influenced by attacker input.

Empirical evaluations of how many vulnerabilities manual vs auto mode let through are not super meaningful because auto mode changes dramatically with model releases, the type of task being performed, whether the attacker is making targeted attacks designed to bypass auto mode, etc. A security feature cannot rely on these sorts of factors if it's to be taken seriously.

Further, percent of malicious tool calls accepted is a bad metric. It's like measuring the security of ssh in terms of what percent of unauthenticated logins succeed. The only acceptable value is zero. It's pass/fail, not a spectrum. So both auto and manual mode should fail equally here. Further, the set of malicious tool calls admitted in auto mode may not be a subset of those admitted in manual mode.

>This is called "approval fatigue".

Doesn't matter, that would be on me.

It's also a false dillema. Those aren't the only options. A strictly enforced sandbox with sane defaults (for example ~/.ssh), that acts as a hard OS level limit, and not just as a suggestion to the agent, would not have "approval fatigue".

Compare approving every step manually: at first you read everything the llm proposes carefully, convinced that you'll catch it out. After a while you get faster and faster until at some point you find yourself hitting "approve" the second the text appears, long before you actually could absorb what it said.

This is called "approval fatigue".

If you think this can't possibly happen to you, you might be in for a surprise. This is an almost textbook case of classic conditioning. You'll find yourself hitting that button faster and faster even while fighting back the urge. So a human is no guaranteed backstop.

This is the scenario that cc auto mode guards against. It cuts down the number of permission prompts to something manageable, so that your fingers don't get trained into clicking 'approve' on 'rm -rf' in the very eyeblink that it appears.

So maybe you feel it doesn't work in theory; but weirdly enough, in practice this particular approach is actually one of the better ones; especially when used in combination with other common sense measures where practical.

Of course, if it's possible to use deterministic automation, I ask it to set up scripts. But in a lot of cases the task is not deterministic. And even when it is, I still need to safely deal with the credentials. Examples of some tasks I use it for:

- Research and buy me a domain name for xyz product, set up all of its DNS the way I want for this product, set up email, set up app store submissions including screenshots and description, set up firebase notifications, set up my Google cloud project and any apis I need to enable for this app, deal with app store review feedback.

- Do an audit of my books, make sure every transaction has a receipt uploaded, and make sure the receipt matches the journal entry. Pull statements from all my my bank accounts and reconcile against my books. Fix mistaken transactions with my confirmation.

- Freely push to my source control, but only to specific branch prefixes (surprised that GitHub, gitlab, gitea, etc don't have this built in already). Merge with my confirmation.

- Freely read the subject lines in my Gmail and full emails from my accountant, freely search emails (but still can't read them), freely compose drafts, ask me to read full emails other than my accountant's, ask me to send drafts. No way for it to read password reset links, for example.

Not to mention that I only have to have a single key that gives access to all my services. If the key leaks, I just have to rotate one key because the agent never has access to the 30 upstream service keys. If I need to give weaker or stronger keys for a specific agent, I can easily configure that in one place (and I can even request that the agent make that change for me with my confirmation). I don't need to create 20 new keys every time, and I don't need to remember the intricacies of every upstream service's UI for creating new keys.

Edit: forgot to mention one more really convenient thing the API proxy enables: I can ask my agent to just configure things for me e.g. changing CI settings, adding Google workspace users or groups, etc. without having to use the to UI. So now nearly all of the admin configuration for all services is done from a single interface (my agent cli)

> At the same time, I want them to take away the tedium of a bunch of tasks I'm required to do, and it sucks to have to micromanage them.

Consider reframing. Is the problem really that the task is tedious? Or that it's required? Maybe you should be leaning more on deterministic automations (which the LLM can help set up) rather than LLM-powered ones.

children.text:
The agent doesn't decide which endpoints are destructive, you do. That's the point. It's not allowed to do anything that you don't explicitly grant permission for.

And yes, it has tried to make bad requests! Which it wasn't able to do because it was either rejected outright or asked me for confirmation and I didn't let it through.

The "surface area" you're talking about is just the coverage of the service APIs, which is there just as a nicety to give a semantic preview of what the request is about to do e.g. we know what a gmail request looks like so we can render a preview of the attachment the agent is sending so you can inspect it. Otherwise you'd have to inspect each http request (which you can always do by using the generic http acl).

I somewhat agree with "exfiltrate enormously sensitive data". The thing I'm paranoid about is catastrophic mistakes that can instantly kill the business e.g. "Oops I sold the domain name". Leaking financials is not great, but also not catastrophic. Deleting all our books would be catastrophic, which the underlying QuickBooks key allows you to do!

But in any case, you can choose your level of paranoia and give exactly the amount of access you're comfortable with. For example, I view read access to emails as catastrophic (must worse than read access to financials), so I don't let it do that.

I'm skeptical of how "super paranoid" you actually are. This doesn't sound super paranoid.

For instance: that's a ton of surface area. Did you have your AI agent decide which endpoint is destructive or did you manually do this?

For instance: has this classification been wrong?

I ask this because I've used a similar thing before and it failed in the ways I've named.

This setup also permits your agent to exfiltrate enormously sensitive data (website gives the example of QuickBooks invoices and Cloudflare config) without your involvement.

I'm super paranoid about the level of access AI agents have. At the same time, I want them to take away the tedium of a bunch of tasks I'm required to do, and it sucks to have to micromanage them.

The best solution I've been able to come up is using an ephemeral vm (on an isolated network) per task, using --dangerously-skip-permissions so it doesn't bother me. I couple that with an API proxy that lets me restrict the permissions it has to external services. So e.g. where a quickbooks API key gives the holder "god mode" access, the proxy lets the agent do certain read commands without confirmation, but all write endpoints except uploading receipts require confirmation on my phone before they'll be allowed to hit the quickbooks servers. I no longer need to trust that the agent will interpret my readonly wishes correctly.

Tooting my own horn here, but this setup works incredibly well! I've been able to connect dozens of services safely where I absolutely do not trust giving raw, overpowered credentials or oauth integration to the agent directly. I actually just released the API proxy today at https://keycontain.com
